\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\title{Three-Dimensional Structural Restoration\\
of a Fault-Propagation Fold in a Foreland Basin}
\author{R. Calloway and I. Mensah}
\date{March 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\section{Setting}
The study anticline sits in the distal foreland of the orogen,
where Mesozoic strata rest on a gently dipping basement unconformity.
Seismic interpretation ties the fold to a blind thrust that dies out
upsection within the shale interval.

\section{Model Construction}
The reservoir interval lies at a true vertical depth of
\SI{3.4}{\kilo\metre}, and the vertical effective stress at that
level reaches \SI{42}{\mega\pascal}.
Bedding on the forelimb dips \ang{58} toward the southeast,
while the backlimb dips \ang{35} in the same direction.
The sealing shale is \SI{260}{\metre} thick at the crest
and thins toward the flanks.
Geothermal modelling sets the reservoir temperature at
\SI{95}{\degreeCelsius}.

\section{Restoration}
The restored section shortens by \SI{1.8}{\kilo\metre} across the
fold, equivalent to roughly 12\% line-length shortening.
Fault heave measured on the interpretation grid is largest near the
fold hinge and decreases toward the lateral tip line.

\section{Validation}
Line-length balancing closes within 3\% across all restored sections.
Area-depth analysis predicts a detachment depth consistent with the
bright reflector package imaged beneath the forelimb.
Residual misfit concentrates where the seismic volume loses
coherence beneath the crestal fault shadow.

\section{Implications}
The restoration constrains the timing of trap formation relative to
charge, and it provides boundary conditions for the geomechanical
model of fracture intensity on the forelimb.

\end{document}
